samples: This program prints a directory tree, indented two spaces per level, with each file's and folder's size in bytes, starting from the directory given on the command line or the current one. It only reads the filesystem and writes to the console, and it lists each folder's children sorted by name. Two cautions: it recomputes folder sizes from scratch at every level, so it will be slow on large trees, and it relies on filesystem features (inspecting entries, the Entry and FileError types, getting a path's name) that the documented standard library doesn't list, so it may not compile as written.

This program prints an indented tree of the directory named on the command line (or the current one), listing every file and folder sorted by name with its size in bytes, where a folder's size is the sum of everything beneath it. It only reads the filesystem and writes to the console, it stops with a file error on the first failure, and it counts anything that is neither a file nor a folder as zero bytes. It recomputes each folder's total at every level, so large or deep trees will be slow. It also depends on entry inspection and path-name features that aren't in the documented standard library list, so confirm they exist before relying on it.

This program prints an indented tree of the directory given as the first command-line argument (or the current directory if none is given). Each file and folder is shown with its size in bytes, folders' sizes being the sum of everything beneath them, and children are listed alphabetically. It only needs to read the filesystem and print to the console, but it stops with an error at the first unreadable entry, and it recalculates each folder's size at every level, so it will be slow on large trees. It also relies on filesystem pieces (inspecting an entry, file/directory distinctions, getting a path's name) that aren't in the library list I know, so check that they exist before depending on it.

This program prints a directory tree, taking the directory from the first command-line argument or using the current one, with each file and folder shown at its depth, children sorted by name, and its size in bytes (folders show the sum of everything beneath them). It only reads the filesystem and prints to the console, and it stops with an error at the first entry it cannot read rather than skipping it. Two caveats before you rely on it: it recomputes each folder's size at every level, so it will be slow on large trees, and it uses filesystem operations (inspecting an entry, getting a path's name) that the standard library list I was given does not include, so it may not work as written.

This program prints an indented tree of a directory, given on the command line or defaulting to the current one, with each file and folder shown with its size in bytes, where folder sizes are the sum of everything beneath them. It only reads the filesystem and writes to the console, but it stops with an error if any entry cannot be read, and it recomputes each folder's size at every level, so deep or large trees will be slower than necessary. Its inspection of entries (file vs. directory vs. other) and its path-name lookup rely on filesystem features that the language's documented library doesn't list, so check that they exist before depending on it.
